page: Microsoft Azure D8ps_v5 is a general-purpose virtual machine based on the ARM64 architecture, powered by an Ampere ARMv8 Neoverse-N1 processor operating at 3.0 GHz. The instance provides 8 dedicated physical cores mapped to 8 vCPUs without simultaneous multithreading, along with 32 GB of system memory, matching a standard 1:4 core-to-memory ratio. Cache allocation includes 64 KB of L1 data cache per core, 1.0 MB of L2 cache per core, and a shared 32 MB L3 cache. Cryptographic processing includes hardware AES acceleration, while standard x86 vector instruction sets are not present on this ARM platform. The instance does not include local disk storage or hardware accelerators like GPUs, relying instead on network-attached Premium Storage.

Benchmark results demonstrate consistent mid-tier performance across multi-threaded and memory-intensive metrics. The Neoverse-N1 architecture achieved 14,501.41 on multi-core stress-ng tests and a Geekbench multi-core score of 5,805.0, reflecting linear scaling across its physical cores. Memory operations show robust throughput, recording 562.63 GB/s on small-block cached reads and 73.72 GB/s on uncached 256 MB reads. In service-oriented workloads, the instance delivered 9.88 million Redis SET operations per second and 10.39 GB/s in static web serving throughput. Software compilation benchmarks using Clang also fell into average performance tiers.

Single-thread performance metrics expose architectural tradeoffs compared to contemporary high-frequency x86 platforms. Geekbench single-core scored 1,030.0, and PassMark single-thread and encryption benchmarks ranked in the lower percentiles. Decompression throughput via bzip3 proved weak in both single-threaded (7.26 GB/s) and multi-threaded (32.83 GB/s) evaluations. Furthermore, language model inference speeds on small models remained low, generating 48.6 tokens per second.

The D8ps_v5 offers an efficient compute-per-core profile for workloads that scale horizontally across physical threads without relying on legacy x86 instructions. It is suited for containerized microservices, web servers, open-source relational and in-memory databases like Redis, Clang compilation pipelines, and general cloud workloads requiring steady multi-core execution.
